extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, theatre-critics, and educated readers interested in dramatic craft and taste
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and staging dramatic works (especially tragedy vs comedy), focusing on what to represent onstage or offstage, effects upon the audience, and tasteful use of theatrical artifices. Rooted in 18th-century critical standards and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evoke pity with family distress (use sparingly)
rubrics_metrics.description: Showing a disconsolate mother with a child, or children accompanying a distressed parent, is an effective device to draw compassion from an audience; successive writers have escalated this (princess with two children, then three children) to increase effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such incidents are 'beautiful in a good Writer, become ridiculous by falling into the Hands of a bad one.' Use family-distress devices with restraint and artistic judgment; avoid mechanical multiplication of children or mawkish doubling that turns pity into ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid public displays of murder and butcheries onstage
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent onstage stabbing, poisoning, rackings, impalements and strewing the stage with carcasses is described as absurd, barbarous, and a sign of a cruel temper in writers who delight in such spectacles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from gratuitous bloodshed meant merely to gratify a love of spectacle—such exposure invites contempt and ridicule and reflects poorly on national taste. Reserve graphic onstage violence only when artistically necessary and handled with decency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transact murders and executions behind the scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: The French theatre generally conducts murders and executions offstage (behind the scenes), a practice commended for civility and decency; ancient practice likewise avoids showing certain violent acts publicly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For crimes of extreme horror (parricide, unnatural murders) prefer offstage execution: have the act occur offstage and report or represent its consequences onstage (cries, reports, produced bodies). This preserves decency and often increases dramatic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forbear to commit parricides or unnatural murders before the audience (Horace's rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted rule: Nec coram populo natos Medea trucidet / 'Let not Medea draw her murth'ring Knife, And spill her Children's Blood upon the Stage.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not represent parricides or similarly shocking unnatural murders directly before the audience; such scenes are better handled offstage or by implication, following Horace's precept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use offstage dialogue and sounds to heighten effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancient examples (Sophocles' Orestes) execute dreadful resolutions offstage but use cries, replies, and reported speech so the audience experiences the horror vividly without seeing the act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ offstage exchanges (a mother calling for mercy, a son answering) and auditory cues to make events more affecting than their explicit display would be; well-crafted offstage dialogue can be 'infinitely more affecting' than onstage action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present bodies after death rather than the killing itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Although killings were often not shown, the ancients frequently produced the bodies after death, which carries melancholy or terror.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the plot requires the audience to confront the reality of a death, consider revealing the body post-event rather than staging the violent act; this retains the emotional weight while avoiding indecency or improbability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid improbability and unnatural representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Killing onstage can appear very unnatural (e.g., killing 'in cold blood' after a prolonged chase across the stage) and contradicts probability and the audience's sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer representations consistent with nature and probability. Do not stage actions that strain credibility or produce an unnatural effect; tell or imply actions when their onstage portrayal would seem improbable or ridiculous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance refinement with dramatic effect (don't banish all kinds of death)
rubrics_metrics.description: Horace and the ancients forbade certain horrid scenes onstage but did not intend to remove all depictions of death; French refinements sometimes go too far in avoiding all kinds of death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek a middle course: spare public executions that would shock or be indecent, but do not banish every manifestation of death if its representation serves the drama. Practice moderation—avoid both barbarous display and over-refinement that ruins effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy permits broader artifices and prop-based characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Ridicule is less delicate than compassion, and comedic inventions (costume, props, physical gags) have a much greater latitude—examples include Bullock in a short coat, Norris in a long one, brimmed hats, shoulder-belts, whiskers, and a lover peeping out of a barrel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use costume, exaggerated props, and bodily comedy more freely in comedy than in tragedy. Because comic objects and devices are numerous and forgiving, they can be exploited to signal character and provoke laughter, but still be mindful of taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive or hackneyed sentimental contrivances
rubrics_metrics.description: There are several dramatick inventions used by ignorant poets to supply the place of true tragedy; some ought to be entirely rejected, others used with caution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of stock sentimental devices that manipulate audience emotions cheaply. Reject those that are obviously contrived or ridiculous; use other artifices sparingly and with subtlety to avoid undermining the work's dignity and credibility.
